1. The Core Meaning: A Taste

The most fundamental meaning of sour describes a sharp, biting, acidic taste — the kind that makes your mouth water, your lips pucker, or your eyes squint slightly.

Think of biting into a raw lemon, a raw tamarind, an unripe green mango, or drinking plain vinegar. That sharp, tangy sensation on your tongue — especially on the sides — is sourness. It is one of the five basic tastes humans can detect, alongside sweet, salty, bitter, and umami (savory).

Sourness comes from acids. Lemons contain citric acid. Vinegar contains acetic acid. Yogurt and buttermilk contain lactic acid. This is why all of these things taste sour — they share the same underlying chemistry.

Sour vs. nearby tastes:

  • Sour is not bitter. Bitter is the unpleasant sharpness of black coffee, neem, or dark chocolate. Sour is the sharp, tangy, acidic quality of citrus and fermented foods. The two are easy to confuse, but they feel different on the tongue and come from different substances.
  • Sour is not spicy. Spiciness is a burning sensation, not a taste at all.
  • Something can be both sour and sweet at the same time — like a ripe kiwi, a mango-chili candy, or a sweet-lime. This is why "sweet and sour" is a common flavor combination in food.

Examples of sour-tasting things:
Lemon, lime, raw tamarind, unripe mango, cranberries, gooseberries (amla), vinegar, curd/yogurt, buttermilk (chaas), sourdough bread, kombucha, raw green apple, kokum.

The degree of sourness matters. Something can be mildly sour (a ripe orange), pleasantly sour (good yogurt), or sharply/harshly sour (straight lemon juice or vinegar). The word itself does not tell you the degree — you understand it from context.

When food or liquid has gone bad — especially through fermentation or rotting — it develops an unpleasant sharp smell. We also call this sour.

Milk that has been left out too long smells sour. Wet laundry left in a bucket for days smells sour. A person with poor dental hygiene may have sour breath.

Notice the connection: when things ferment or decay, they produce acids. Those same acids responsible for a sour taste in fresh lemons are now responsible for a sour smell in spoiled milk. This is why the same word covers both. When something smells sour, it usually signals that it has spoiled or is no longer fresh.
3. Sour as a Human Mood or Expression

A person, their face, or their mood can be described as sour. Here, the meaning shifts from taste to emotion — but the connection is clear: just as a sour taste is unpleasant and sharp, a sour person is unpleasant to deal with.

A sour person is someone who is bitter, unhappy, grumpy, or resentful in a persistent, sulky way. They are not fun to be around. They complain, find fault, or simply carry an air of bitterness about them. It is different from someone who is merely sad — a sour person is often unpleasant to others because of their bitterness.

A sour expression or sour look means a facial expression that shows displeasure, resentment, or disapproval — like someone who has just tasted something they dislike. If someone gives you a sour look when you walk in, they are showing clear disapproval without saying a word.

A sour mood means someone is in an irritable, sullen, bad-tempered state at that moment.

"Why is he so sour today? Did something happen?"
"She gave me a sour look when I arrived late."
"Don't mind him — he's always a bit sour in the mornings."
4. Sour as a Way to Describe Situations Gone Wrong

When something that was once positive, promising, or pleasant turns bad, we say it has gone sour or turned sour. This is a very common and natural way to use the word.

"Their friendship turned sour after the argument."
"The business deal went sour when both parties stopped trusting each other."
"What started as a great working relationship eventually turned sour."

The imagery is intuitive: just as fresh milk turns sour when it spoils, good situations turn sour when they deteriorate.

In farming, sour soil (also called sour land) means soil that is excessively acidic — that is, soil with a low pH. Such soil is poor for growing most crops. Farmers "sweeten" sour soil by adding lime (calcium carbonate) to reduce the acidity. This is a more specialized use of the word, but the logic is the same: acidity = sourness.

This is a well-known expression worth knowing. When someone cannot get or achieve something they wanted, and then pretends they did not want it anyway, we call that sour grapes.

The phrase comes from an old fable about a fox who tries to reach grapes hanging high on a vine. After failing to reach them, the fox walks away saying the grapes were probably sour anyway. He is rationalizing his failure — convincing himself he did not want something he actually did.

"He said the job was not worth having, but that sounds like sour grapes to me — he applied for it three times."

The word sour carries a consistent thread through all its meanings: something sharp, unpleasant, and acidic — whether that is a taste on your tongue, a smell in the air, a person's personality, or a situation that has deteriorated. When something is sour, something has gone wrong, gone too far, or curdled from what it should be.
